chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Financial Statements Matter to Managers

lessons.title: Financial Statements Explained: The Scorecard Every Manager Is Judged By

children.text: It is the quarterly business review at Kesari Foods, a fictional Indore-based snacks company. Rohan, the national sales head, opens with good news: revenue is up 18%, the best quarter in three years. The CFO nods, then asks one question: "Then why did we have to draw ₹4 crore from our cash credit line last month?" Rohan has no answer. The room moves on, and so does the budget he wanted for next quarter.

Rohan is not bad at his job. He simply reads one number, while the people who approve budgets read three statements at once. This lesson shows you what those three statements are, what each one answers, and why every decision you make at work ends up as a line in one of them.

body.text: Every decision a manager makes, from a discount to a hire to a new laptop order, eventually shows up as a line in the financial statements. Learn to read them and you learn how your company keeps score of you.

children.text: What Financial Statements Actually Are

Financial statements are a company's formal report card, prepared in a standard format so that anyone, from a bank to a board member to a new manager, can read them the same way. In India, Section 2(40) of the Companies Act, 2013 lists what they include:
Balance sheet
as at the end of the financial year
Profit and loss statement
for the financial year
Cash flow statement
for the financial year
Statement of changes in equity
, where applicable
Notes
that explain and break down all of the above

This course focuses on the first three, because they are the ones discussed in every review meeting. Indian companies prepare them for a financial year running from 1 April to 31 March, which is why you hear "FY25" for the year ended 31 March 2025. Listed companies and larger unlisted ones follow
Ind AS
, which Lesson 1.3 covers.

markDefs.definition: Indian Accounting Standards, the Indian version of the global IFRS rules, notified under the Companies Act. Smaller unlisted companies follow the older Accounting Standards (AS) issued by ICAI.

body.text: One Person Companies, small companies, dormant companies and private companies that are start-ups can leave out the cash flow statement. So if you work at an early-stage startup and see only a P&L and balance sheet, that is legal. It is also exactly why founders get surprised by cash crunches.

children.text: Three Statements, Three Questions
The fastest way to keep the three apart is to remember the one question each statement answers.

cells: Profit and loss statement (P&L)
Did we make money this year?
A period, e.g. 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025
Your salary slip for the year: what came in, what was deducted
Balance sheet
What do we own, what do we owe, and what is left for the owners?
A single date, e.g. 31 March 2025
A photo of your net worth on one day: flat, car loan, savings
Cash flow statement
Where did the actual cash come from and go?
A period, same as the P&L
Your bank statement, grouped by type of transaction

children.text: Two formulas sit underneath everything in this course. You will meet them again and again.

columns.label: P&L and cash flow statement: a video
points: Cover a full period, usually a quarter or a year
Numbers add up over the period
Start again from zero next year

columns.label: Balance sheet: a photograph
points: Captured on one date, usually 31 March
Numbers are balances on that day

body.title: Video or photo?
body.textWithBlank: The balance sheet shows a company's position at a single point in ___, while the P&L covers a period.
body.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot on one date, such as 31 March 2025. The P&L and cash flow statement both cover a period, such as the full financial year.

trade receivables
and
trade payables

Money the company owes its suppliers for goods or services already received.

body.caption: Kesari Foods: what changed on the balance sheet during FY25

cells: Trade receivables (distributors owe us more)
Up ₹6 crore
Cash not yet collected: minus ₹6 crore
Inventory (more stock in warehouses)
Up ₹1 crore
Cash spent on stock not yet sold: minus ₹1 crore
Trade payables (we owe suppliers more)
Up ₹3 crore
Cash not yet paid out: plus ₹3 crore

stats.label: Stuck with distributors
stats.context: Created by longer credit terms to hit sales targets

children.text: Rohan's team hit its revenue number partly by giving distributors 60 days of credit instead of 30. That decision looked brilliant on the P&L, harmless on his dashboard, and painful on the balance sheet and cash flow statement. Every statement was telling the truth. He was reading only one of them.

body.text: Revenue is recorded when you deliver and bill, not when the customer pays. A manager who is measured only on revenue can quietly drain the company's cash while looking like a star. Finance teams know this, which is why they ask about receivables the moment sales numbers look unusually good.

body.title: Profit vs cash
body.prompt: Another year, Kesari Foods reports a profit of ₹12 crore. Trade receivables rise by ₹9 crore, inventory is unchanged, and trade payables rise by ₹2 crore. Ignoring tax and depreciation, what is cash from operations, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹12 crore profit, minus ₹9 crore extra receivables, plus ₹2 crore extra payables = ₹5 crore. More than half the profit is still sitting with customers.

The same three statements exist at every Indian company, from Kesari Foods to Infosys. Here are a few headline numbers from Infosys' consolidated statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, as shown on screener.in.

stats.label: Cash from operations (cash flow)

children.text: Notice that Infosys generated more operating cash than profit, the opposite of Kesari Foods. For a mature services company with disciplined collections, that is normal and healthy. Chapter 4 explains every reason the two numbers differ.

body.title: Which statement would you open?
body.question: Your CFO asks how much Kesari Foods owes its banks on 31 March 2025. Which statement answers this directly?
options: None of them, you must ask the bank
body.explanation: Borrowings outstanding on a specific date are a liability, and liabilities sit on the balance sheet. The P&L shows only the interest cost for the year, and the cash flow statement shows how much was borrowed or repaid during the year, not the balance owed.

children.text: Why Managers Are Judged by These Numbers

You may never prepare a financial statement, but your department writes several of its lines every single day. Leadership reads these statements to decide targets, budgets, headcount and bonuses, so it helps to know which lines carry your fingerprints.

cells: Sales
Offer distributors 60-day credit to close a deal
Revenue on the P&L; trade receivables on the balance sheet; lower operating cash
HR and L&D
Approve annual increments and a leadership programme
Employee benefit expense and other expenses on the P&L; salaries paid in operating cash
Procurement
Buy six months of packaging to lock in a price
Inventory on the balance sheet; cash outflow now, expense only as stock is used
Operations and IT
Buy a new packing line or 300 laptops
Fixed assets on the balance sheet; investing cash outflow; depreciation on the P&L over several years
Treasury
Draw ₹4 crore from the cash credit line
Borrowings on the balance sheet; financing cash inflow; interest cost on the P&L

body.title: The increment approval
body.scenario: You head HR at a Pune-based IT services firm with 200 employees on an average annual CTC of ₹8 lakh. The leadership team is considering a 10% across-the-board increment from 1 April. The CEO asks you to explain the impact "in finance language" before the board meeting.
body.prompt: Which statements are affected, by roughly how much per year, and what would you flag?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Size of the change: 200 × ₹8 lakh × 10% = ₹1.6 crore of extra cost per year.
2. P&L: employee benefit expense rises by about ₹1.6 crore a year, which lowers profit by the same amount before tax, unless revenue grows to cover it.
3. Cash flow statement: operating cash falls by roughly the same amount, since salaries are paid monthly in cash. Employer PF and gratuity contributions linked to basic pay add a little more.
4. Balance sheet: little changes directly, but lower profit means slower growth in retained earnings, and any unpaid bonus or leave provisions at year end appear as liabilities.
5. What to flag: the increment is permanent and compounds every year, while a one-time bonus is not. Suggest comparing ₹1.6 crore against expected revenue growth and attrition costs.

body.title: Who prepares and checks these statements?

children.text: Knowing who stands behind the numbers helps you trust them, and question them.
Finance and accounts team:
records transactions and prepares the statements, usually under the CFO.
Board of directors:
approves the financial statements. Under Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013, they must give a true and fair view and follow the notified accounting standards.
Statutory auditor:
an independent chartered accountant firm that checks the statements and issues an audit report every year.
Shareholders:
adopt the audited statements at the annual general meeting.
Regulators:
companies file statements with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), and listed companies also publish results on NSE and BSE under SEBI's disclosure rules.

body.title: Before your next review meeting
steps: Write down the one metric your team is measured on (revenue, cost, headcount, uptime).
Name the financial statement line that metric feeds into.
Identify one decision your team made this quarter that affects cash differently from profit.
If your employer is listed, open its page on screener.in and find last year's revenue, net profit and cash from operations.
Prepare one question to ask your finance business partner about how your team's numbers are read.

cards.definition: A company's formal annual report card: balance sheet, P&L, cash flow statement, statement of changes in equity and notes.
Shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period. Answers "did we make money?"
Shows assets, liabilities and equity on a single date. Answers "where do we stand?"
Shows actual cash coming in and going out over a period, grouped into operating, investing and financing.
In India, 1 April to 31 March. FY25 ends on 31 March 2025.
Money customers owe for goods or services already billed.
Indian Accounting Standards, based on IFRS, followed by listed and larger companies.

points: Financial statements are a standard-format report card: balance sheet, P&L, cash flow statement, statement of changes in equity and notes.
The P&L asks "did we make money?", the balance sheet asks "where do we stand?", and the cash flow statement asks "where did the cash go?"
The P&L and cash flow statement cover a period. The balance sheet is a snapshot on one date.
Profit and cash are different. Extra credit to customers can lift revenue and profit while draining cash.
Every department writes lines in these statements, which is why leadership uses them to set budgets and judge performance.

body.text: Kesari Foods and the Pune IT services firm are fictional and used for illustration. Infosys figures are consolidated FY25 numbers as shown on screener.in and are rounded for teaching. This lesson is for education only.
